strengths: The paper targets an important gap: systematic evaluation of geometric and 3D spatial capabilities in multimodal language models, beyond conventional semantic spatial questions.

VGBench contributes 6,000 questions covering camera parameters, pose, homography, depth, distance, reconstruction, tracking, and object position. The use of annotated 3D datasets provides a scalable basis for generating geometry-focused questions.

SpatialScore offers broad coverage by consolidating 28,093 samples from VGBench and 11 prior datasets across single-image, multi-image, and video inputs and three answer formats. Evaluating 25 open models from 1B to 78B produces a useful empirical snapshot.

SpatialAgent combines established perception and geometry models with both Plan-Execute and ReAct orchestration. On SpatialScore-Hard, the strongest configuration raises its InternVL3-8B core from 12.86% to 46.08%, suggesting that explicit geometric tools can materially help on at least the selected tasks.

The appendix provides substantial implementation information, including question-generation templates, model prompts, tool interfaces, dataset composition, and per-source results. The main paper is visually clear, and the authors include qualitative failure cases rather than showing only successes.
weaknesses: The central SpatialAgent evidence is confounded by evaluation only on SpatialScore-Hard. This subset was selected specifically where at least 16 of 20 baseline MLLMs failed, whereas agent-assisted systems were not part of the selection. The resulting reversal—many 32B–78B models score only 12–22%—is therefore expected from selection bias and cannot support general claims that the agent surpasses larger or proprietary models. SpatialAgent results on the full SpatialScore, VGBench, and independently selected held-out data are absent.

The agent study lacks controls needed to attribute its gains. There is no comparison against the same core model with matched reasoning prompts and test-time compute, deterministic task-specific pipelines, individual expert tools, or oracle tool selection; nor are tool invocation success, latency, and computational cost reported. Because several tools directly estimate the target quantities, the results establish benefits of access to specialist predictors more clearly than benefits of the proposed multi-agent orchestration.

Benchmark validity is insufficiently demonstrated. VGBench contains 6,000 correlated questions from only about 300 scenes, but the paper reports no scene-disjoint protocol, duplicate analysis, systematic human audit, annotator agreement, or error rate. Manual verification is described only for the hard subset and without annotator counts or agreement. Training contamination is acknowledged but not measured, despite extensive reuse of established public benchmarks and ScanNet-derived material.

Some VGBench tasks are not well posed from the stated visual inputs. Absolute intrinsics in pixel units, world-coordinate 3D boxes, and metric camera translations are generally not identifiable from RGB images without scale and coordinate conventions. Questions about distances between objects use centroid distance even when wording can imply surface separation, and average depth over a 2D box may mix the object with background. The paper does not establish that these ambiguities were controlled.

The aggregate score mixes heterogeneous protocols and is sample-weighted, so large sources dominate the result. A factor-of-two tolerance for metric answers is very permissive, while single-image-only models receive only the first frame for multi-frame/video tasks and are consequently evaluated on missing information. These choices make overall rankings difficult to interpret; uncertainty intervals and scene-level statistics are also absent despite within-scene dependence.

Reproducibility is weakened by internal inconsistencies. For example, a qualitative trace calls EstimateObjectDepth with bounding boxes and a mode argument, although its declared interface requires object descriptions and has no mode; the standard RAFT flow direction is also described with an apparently reversed object-motion sign unless an undocumented convention is used. Code and data are only promised, not provided in the manuscript.

The claimed methodological originality is modest: SpatialScore is mostly an aggregation of existing benchmarks, and SpatialAgent composes existing vision models using standard Plan-Execute/ReAct patterns. The manuscript also claims that models lag humans without reporting a human baseline. Minor presentation issues such as repeated superlatives, typographical errors, and incomplete qualitative entries are secondary to the evaluation and validity concerns above.

strengths: The paper targets an important CV problem: evaluating geometric and spatial capabilities that are poorly captured by general-purpose MLLM benchmarks.

VGBench adds 6,000 questions derived from 3D annotations across eight geometry-oriented task families, including pose, homography, depth, tracking, and camera parameters. SpatialScore further assembles 28,093 examples from 12 sources with single-image, multi-image, and video inputs.

The empirical survey is broad, covering 25 open-source models from 1B to 78B parameters, with additional proprietary-model results on SpatialScore-Hard. The per-category tables reveal useful failure patterns rather than reporting only an aggregate score.

The appendix provides question-generation templates, evaluation prompts, tool interfaces, and data-source counts, which improves clarity and could support reproducibility if the promised code and data are released.

SpatialAgent produces substantial gains on SpatialScore-Hard: for example, the InternVL-based Plan-Execute variant reaches 46.08% versus 12.86% for InternVL3-8B, demonstrating that specialized vision tools can materially help on these questions.
weaknesses: The central SpatialScore-Hard comparison is methodologically biased. The subset is explicitly selected because at least 16 of 20 evaluated MLLMs fail each example, and many of those same models are then evaluated on it. Their very low and non-monotonic scores are therefore partly guaranteed by construction, whereas SpatialAgent was not used in selection. This makes the claimed superiority over existing MLLMs difficult to interpret as an unbiased performance comparison.

SpatialAgent is technically incremental: it applies standard Plan-Execute or ReAct prompting to a collection of existing models and classical tools such as DepthAnythingV2, VGGT, RAFT, SIFT, SAM2, and OWLv2. Calling the planner/executor/summarizer arrangement a novel multi-agent system is not well justified, and the work does not isolate a new agent algorithm.

The agent evaluation lacks essential controls. SpatialAgent is reported only on the selected hard subset, not the full VGBench or SpatialScore, and there are no single-tool, oracle-routing, random-routing, prompt-only, or matched-compute baselines. Consequently, the results do not establish whether gains arise from orchestration, direct use of task-specific estimators, or benchmark/tool overlap.

Several VGBench tasks are not identifiable from the supplied visual evidence alone. Absolute metric scale, world-coordinate 3D boxes, and camera intrinsics generally cannot be uniquely recovered from an unconstrained RGB image. Performance can therefore reflect learned priors or multiple-choice elimination rather than visual-geometric understanding. Synthetic homographies and numerically constructed distractors may likewise admit shortcuts, but no shortcut audit is presented.

The evidence for dataset quality is insufficient. Although the 1,400 hard examples are said to be manually verified, the paper gives no number or expertise of annotators, annotation protocol, rejection statistics, inter-annotator agreement, or category-level error audit. The broader 6,000-example VGBench appears largely template-generated and receives no reported human validation.

SpatialScore combines heterogeneous datasets, question formats, chance levels, and scoring rules into a sample-weighted accuracy. It also changes some source protocols, such as MMVP question-level scoring to sample-level scoring and VSI-Bench continuous scoring to a factor-of-two correctness threshold. Without dataset-normalized scores, calibration, or sensitivity analysis, the single overall number is not a well-founded unified measure.

A factor-of-two tolerance for metric answers is extremely permissive and can obscure large geometric errors. The paper reports neither alternative thresholds nor continuous error metrics, confidence intervals, repeated runs, or significance tests.

The manuscript claims that current MLLMs lag behind humans, but no human baseline is reported. It also attributes agent gains decisively to structured tool invocation despite lacking the ablations needed to support that causal statement.

Contamination and independence are inadequately controlled. Most of SpatialScore reuses public benchmarks, VGBench draws from public reconstruction datasets, and the authors only reduce rather than eliminate ScanNet content. There is no scene-level split specification, duplicate analysis across constituent datasets, or assessment of whether evaluated MLLMs and specialist tools were trained on the source data.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: code and data are only promised for future release, while exact checkpoints, parser implementations, API versions/dates, per-tool preprocessing, runtime, and computational cost are not fully reported. These omissions are material because parsing failures and a nine-tool pipeline can strongly affect both accuracy and fairness.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and under-evaluated capability of multimodal models: metric and geometric spatial understanding beyond ordinary semantic question answering.

VGBench is a useful contribution, providing 6,000 questions across homography, pose, camera intrinsics, reconstruction, depth, distance, tracking, and 3D object position, with ground truth derived from annotated 3D datasets rather than solely from language-model judgments.

SpatialScore offers unusually broad coverage: 28,093 samples drawn from VGBench and 11 existing benchmarks, spanning single-image, multi-image, and video inputs and multiple question formats. The source, modality, and format counts are documented in the appendix.

The empirical study is extensive, evaluating 25 open-source models from 1B to 78B parameters and reporting category-level results. The results reveal informative patterns, including weak performance on homography and metric depth and inconsistent benefits from model scaling or spatial fine-tuning.

SpatialAgent demonstrates that established vision tools can substantially improve spatial QA: on SpatialScore-Hard, the reported Plan-Execute variants reach 35.30% with the Qwen core and 46.08% with the InternVL core, compared with 15.21% and 12.86% for the corresponding direct models. Prompts and tool interfaces are described in considerable detail, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The principal SpatialAgent comparison is confounded by construction of SpatialScore-Hard. The same Qwen2.5-VL-7B and InternVL3-8B base models used as agent cores participated in selecting examples that at least 16 of 20 models answered incorrectly. Their low direct scores are therefore partly guaranteed by selection, while the tool-augmented variants were not selection models. Evaluating the agents on the full SpatialScore or an independently selected test set is necessary to substantiate the magnitude of the claimed improvement.

There are no ablations isolating the contribution of orchestration from that of the expert tools. Results for individual tools, fixed tool pipelines, oracle tool selection, PE/ReAct without tools, and comparable single-agent tool use are absent. Consequently, the evidence does not establish that the proposed multi-agent organization, rather than simply access to strong geometry models, causes the gains.

Potential training or benchmark leakage through the expert tools is not analyzed. VGBench is constructed from ScanNet, ScanNet++, CA-1M, and WildRGB-D, but the paper does not establish whether VGGT, DepthAnythingV2, OWLv2, SAM2, or the other tools were trained on overlapping scenes or datasets.

Some VGBench questions have questionable perceptual identifiability. For example, exact camera intrinsics with very close numerical distractors and metric 3D distances are generally not uniquely recoverable from an uncalibrated RGB image. The paper does not provide human performance, ambiguity analysis, chance baselines, or inter-annotator agreement to validate that these tasks measure spatial understanding rather than guessing or dataset priors.

The hard-set manual verification procedure lacks the number and qualifications of annotators, agreement statistics, and explicit acceptance criteria. This matters because the subset drives the headline agent conclusions and displays unusual inverse-scaling behavior induced by its selection rule.

SpatialAgent largely combines standard Plan-Execute/ReAct prompting with existing vision modules, so its algorithmic originality is limited. Its computational cost, latency, average tool calls, and failure rates are also unreported, preventing assessment of the accuracy-efficiency tradeoff.

The claim that current models lag behind humans is unsupported because no human baseline is reported. The manuscript is otherwise readable, but several strong claims such as “most comprehensive” and “decisive advantages” should be qualified more carefully.
